summary: Defines the MIME content type Message/CPIM, a message format for protocols that conform to the Common Profile for Instant Messaging. It wraps a message with headers describing sender, recipient and other details so it can pass between systems.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a standard envelope for chat messages. The outside shows who sent it and who it is for, no matter which chat app made it.

questions: how are control characters escaped in cpim headers
why must cpim messages be immutable
subtitle: A strict, immutable envelope for instant messages, so signatures survive a trip across different chat systems.

tldr.problem: Different instant messaging systems need to exchange messages through gateways while keeping end-to-end signatures and encryption intact. Ordinary email-style headers can be rewritten in transit, which breaks signatures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3862 defines the MIME type Message/CPIM: a message with a strictly formatted block of metadata headers, then a blank line, then an encapsulated MIME body. Headers use UTF-8, one per line, and must not be modified or reordered.
tldr.outcome: It gives CPIM-compliant protocols one canonical format that security mechanisms can be applied to. It is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 3862 is a Proposed Standard from August 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text describes its use with CPIM instant messaging and presence, and says other applications may reuse the format.

sections.title: Why a Common Message Format
sections.content:
RFC 3862 defines the MIME content type Message/CPIM, a message format for protocols that conform to the Common Profile for Instant Messaging (CPIM). CPIM describes how diverse instant messaging protocols can interwork through gateways. To meet the security requirements of RFC 2779, a common message format is needed so that end-to-end signatures and encryption can be applied.

The format is a canonical one on which signatures are calculated. It stays agnostic about which security mechanism is used. Although it was prepared for CPIM, the RFC says it is general enough to be reused by other applications with similar requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine kids at different schools passing notes through a middleman. They all agree on one note layout so a secret stamp on the note can still be checked at the other end.

sections.title: Problems With Plain Email Headers
sections.content:
Instant messaging protocols must be able to carry a MIME payload, so an email-like syntax seemed natural. The RFC lists why pure RFC 2822/MIME is a poor base for signing:

  • Irregular lexical structure: a value can be encoded in several ways, but a signature needs a single encoding.
  • Weak internationalization: header values must be 7-bit ASCII.
  • Mutability: gateways often rebuild messages in transit, which obliterates most attempts at security.
  • No clear split between message metadata and message content.
  • Limited extensibility, with X-headers as the usual workaround, and no structured values.

The new format keeps a syntax that is generally compatible with RFC 2822/MIME parsers but is simpler and stricter. Its goals include a simple, regular, easily parsed syntax, a compact format for simple messages and a clear separation of metadata from content.
sections.plainLanguage: Email labels can be written many ways and mail handlers like to re-write them. That is bad if you want to prove nobody tampered with the label, so this format allows only one way to write it.

sections.title: Structure of a Message/CPIM Object
sections.content:
A Message/CPIM object is a two-part entity. The first part holds the message metadata headers and the second part is the message content. The parts are separated from the enclosing MIME header fields, and from each other, by blank lines. The only required MIME header on the outer message is Content-type: Message/CPIM.

The metadata headers carry information for the end-to-end transfer from sender to receiver. They MUST NOT be modified, reformatted or reordered in transit, although a CPIM message transfer protocol MAY examine them. The content part is any MIME object, and its headers MUST include at least a Content-Type header.

The end of the message body is defined by the framing mechanism of whatever protocol carries it.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has two parts: a label on the outside and the letter inside. A blank line marks where one stops and the other starts.

sections.title: Header Syntax and Escaping
sections.content:
Each header is written as Key: Value. The rules are strict:

  • One header per line, on a single line, with no whitespace at the start or end of the line.
  • UTF-8 throughout, and each line ends with CR,LF (13,10).
  • Exactly one space character (32) after the name and colon.
  • Header names are case-sensitive, so From: and from: differ. Names are US-ASCII, and the character "." is reserved as a namespace prefix separator.
  • Repeated header names are allowed unless a header's own definition says otherwise. Unrecognized headers should be ignored, except for those named in a Require header.

Control characters must not appear in a header. They are written with a Java-style escape: \uxxxx with exactly four hexadecimal digits, plus short forms such as \\, \t, \n and \r. Only the characters the RFC lists must be escaped, and all others MUST NOT be.

A header can name its language with a parameter, for example Subject:;lang=fr. Without one, human-readable text is assumed to be in language i-default. The RFC gives the full grammar in ABNF.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are like a very fussy form: one answer per line, exact spacing, and special codes for any odd characters, so every computer reads it the same way.

sections.title: Headers, Namespaces and Require
sections.content:
The RFC defines a core set of headers, all in the namespace urn:ietf:params:cpim-headers:: From, To, cc, DateTime, Subject, NS and Require. From, To and cc take an optional formal name and a URI, and To and cc may be repeated for several recipients. DateTime uses a profile of ISO 8601 and helps a recipient guard against replay attacks.

For extension, headers belong to a namespace identified by a globally unique absolute URI. The NS header declares a prefix for it, and the prefix must be declared before it is used. A prefix is local to its message. An NS header with no prefix sets a default namespace.

A sender can insist that the recipient understands something with a Require header, which lists header names separated by commas. The RFC warns that indiscriminate use of Require could harm interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can add their own special fields as long as they put their own unique name tag on them. A sender can also write "you must understand this field" if it really matters.

sections.title: A Worked Example and Signing
sections.content:
The RFC's example message has a From, a To, a DateTime, two Subject headers (one tagged lang=fr), an NS declaration, a Require header and two extension headers. After a blank line comes a text/xml body.

To secure such a message, an application can wrap it in a MIME multipart/signed structure using RFC 1847 with a scheme such as S/MIME or OpenPGP. The RFC shows the same message signed with S/MIME and pkcs7.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a note from Piglet to Eeyore about the weather. To prove it is really from Piglet, the whole note can be sealed with a signature.

sections.title: Immutability and Application Rules
sections.content:
Messages must be treated as immutable once created. An intermediate gateway MUST NOT change the content in any way: no changed or reordered headers, no changed transfer encoding, no changed languages. A transfer agent that wants to make a change should create a new Message/CPIM message that carries the original as its content, like adding a sheet to a bill of lading.

If a transport is not 8-bit clean, the whole message must be tunnelled and unencapsulated at the far end with no data loss. Applying MIME base64 is given as one way to do that. The format is meant for 8-bit clean environments, and any transfer encoding must be exactly reversed before processing signed content.

An application that adopts the format must specify the headers that must be recognized, the headers that must be present, which headers may repeat and how to read them, and its security mechanisms. The IANA registrations cover the Message/CPIM media type and the urn:ietf:params:cpim-headers: URN sub-namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper wants to change a sealed letter, it must put the old letter in a new envelope and add its own note, never scribble on the original.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE MESSAGE FROM RFC 3862, WITHOUT ITS PER-LINE TAGS

data.title: A Message/CPIM message
data.code:
Content-type: Message/CPIM

From: MR SANDERS <im:piglet@100akerwood.com>
To: Depressed Donkey <im:eeyore@100akerwood.com>
DateTime: 2000-12-13T13:40:00-08:00
Subject: the weather will be fine today
Subject:;lang=fr beau temps prevu pour aujourd'hui
NS: MyFeatures <mid:MessageFeatures@id.foo.com>
Require: MyFeatures.VitalMessageOption
MyFeatures.VitalMessageOption: Confirmation-requested
MyFeatures.WackyMessageOption: Use-silly-font

Content-type: text/xml; charset=utf-8
Content-ID: <1234567890@foo.com>

<body>
Here is the text of my message.
</body>
